title: Business Environment
summary: Business environment is the total surroundings (external forces, factors and institutions beyond the business's control: customers, competitors, suppliers, government and social, political, legal and technological factors) that have a direct or indirect bearing on the functioning of a business. Features: sum total of all external factors; micro (specific: investors, competitors, customers) and macro (general: social, political, cultural, legal, technological) factors; inter-relatedness; dynamic (keeps changing); uncertainty (changes are unpredictable); complexity (differs from place to place and country to country).

Importance: determining opportunities and threats; giving direction for growth (Reliance launched Jio seeing the potential of mobile phones); continuous learning; image building (captive power plants during power shortage); meeting competition; identifying the firm's strengths and weaknesses.

Economic environment: economic conditions (GDP, per capita income, availability of capital, foreign exchange reserve), economic policies (industrial, fiscal – public expenditure, taxation and public debt, monetary – credit supply, foreign investment, export-import or Exim policy) and economic system (capitalist, socialist, mixed; India has a mixed economy). Non-economic environment: social (customs, traditions, values, beliefs, literacy, life expectancy), political (political system, government stability, attitude to business, trade unions), legal (laws and regulations such as the Companies Act 2013, FEMA 1999, Factories Act 1948, Consumer Protection Act 2019, Trade Marks Act 1999, Competition Act 2002, Environment Protection Act 1986), technological (methods and techniques of production and distribution; appliances designed for 220 volts in India and 110 volts in USA), demographic (size, density, distribution and growth rate of population) and natural (geographical and ecological factors such as resources and climate; sugar factories near sugarcane).
## Recent developments in the Indian economy

The 1991 reforms abolished industrial licensing in most cases, allowed private participation, carried out disinvestment and opened up the economy; the Foreign Investment Promotion Board was set up. Liberalisation: eliminating unnecessary controls and restrictions (abolishing licensing, freedom to fix prices, simplified import-export procedures, lower tax rates). Privatisation: reducing the role of the public sector by involving the private sector (reducing industries reserved for the public sector from 17 to 8 and later 3, disinvestment, MOU system). Globalisation: integrating the economy with the world economy: free flow of goods, services, capital, technology and labour (lower customs duties, removal of quotas, foreign investment). Impact on business: rapidly changing technology, more demanding consumers, increasing competition, necessity for change and developing human resources.

Goods and Services Tax (GST) from 1 July 2017 ('One nation, one tax'): an indirect tax on the supply of goods and services replacing many indirect taxes; benefits: no tax on tax, technology-driven online procedures, lower cost of goods, faster taxation, fewer compliances, regularises the unorganised sector. Make in India (launched September 2014 by DIPP): objectives include expansion of job opportunities, ease of doing business, upgradation of technology, eliminating unnecessary laws, improving India's global ranking, simpler bureaucratic procedures, transparent and accountable government and boosting economic growth; focus on 25 sectors. Digital India (July 2015): three components – digital infrastructure, delivering government services digitally, and digital literacy; benefits include e-education, e-health, e-sign and DigiLocker, empowerment, easy access to information, improved services, less documentation and employment in IT.

Social responsibility (corporate social responsibility, CSR) is the obligation to act in a manner that serves the best interests of society; it is voluntary, unlike legal obligation; large companies must spend at least 2 per cent of their profits on CSR. Reasons: self-interest, balancing social power, creation of society, social awareness, public image, moral justification. Responsibilities: towards shareholders (safety of investment, regular information, fair dividend, capital appreciation, protect assets); employees (fair wages, good working conditions, housing and medical care, sense of belonging, co-operation); consumers (regular supply, reasonable prices, standard quality, true advertisements, prompt service); government (obey laws, pay taxes honestly and on time, no corrupt practices, discourage monopoly); community (protect environment, employment, preserve culture, help weaker sections, national integration). Environmental pollution: air, water, land and noise pollution; need for pollution control. Business ethics are the moral principles that decide what is right and wrong in business (fair prices, correct weights, prompt taxes, safe products, fair treatment of workers, no black marketing or hoarding).

sa: Explain the importance of business environment (any three points).
It helps determine opportunities and threats, gives direction for growth, supports continuous learning, builds image and helps meet competition.
Explain the impact of government policy changes of 1991 on business.
Companies adopted world-class technology, customers became more demanding, competition from MNCs increased, businesses had to change policies and had to develop human resources.
It eliminates tax on tax, is technology driven and online, lowers the cost of goods, speeds up taxation, reduces compliances and regularises the unorganised sector.
Explain the responsibilities of business towards consumers.
Regular supply, reasonable prices, standard quality, true advertisements and prompt service and attention to complaints.
Distinguish between social responsibility and legal obligation, and give three reasons for social responsibility.
Legal obligation is followed for fear of law; social responsibility is voluntary. Reasons: self-interest, public image and moral justification.
la: Explain the dimensions of business environment (economic and non-economic) with examples.

Economic: conditions, policies and system (mixed economy). Non-economic: social (customs, literacy), political (stability), legal (Companies Act 2013), technological, demographic and natural environment, each influencing business decisions.
Why is it significant for a business to understand its environment?
It identifies opportunities and threats, gives direction for growth, enables continuous learning, builds image, helps meet competition and shows strengths and weaknesses.
Explain liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation and their impact on business.

Liberalisation removes controls; privatisation reduces the public sector's role; globalisation integrates the economy with the world; effects: technological change, demanding consumers, competition, need for change and human resource development.
Explain the social responsibility of business towards different interest groups.
Towards owners (fair return), employees (fair wages), consumers (quality goods), government (taxes and laws) and the community (environment, employment, culture).
